title: Commentary on the Mishnah
hook: written in Arabic while he was still young and wandering

segments.voice: Yesterday, the saying about Maimonides, and your line: from Moses to Moses. Which great teacher came to mind when you thought of one? Today, the book where his own teaching began. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A long book, and at the very end of it, an apology. Maimonides closes one of his early books by asking the reader for patience. He wrote it, he says, while his mind was troubled and while he was on the move, some of it on the road and some of it at sea. So if you find a mistake, he asks, judge him kindly. Then look at what he had taken on while traveling: the Mishnah, the core text of the oral law, explained passage by passage. He says he wrote it while he was still young. Today, the book that started him.
screen: `AN APOLOGY AT THE END.` → `WRITTEN ON THE ROAD AND AT SEA.` → `THE MISHNAH, PASSAGE BY PASSAGE.`

segments.voice: Commentary on the Mishnah. In Hebrew, Perush HaMishnayot. Turn it four ways. First, the language. Maimonides wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, set down in Hebrew letters. He wanted it read and used, not admired. Hebrew translations came later, and those are what readers of the Hebrew page meet today. Second, the method. The Mishnah is terse. It often starts in the middle of an argument, as if you already know what the argument is about. Maimonides goes passage by passage and asks the beginner's questions. What is this about? What does this word mean? Which view is the law? Then he gives the bottom line, plainly. Third, the doorways. Before some sections he wrote long introductions that read like books of their own. One opens the whole Mishnah and explains how the oral tradition was handed down. One, on a chapter of tractate Sanhedrin, sets out the foundations of Jewish belief. One, before Pirkei Avot, is about the health of the soul. In the days ahead we'll walk through two of those doorways. Fourth, the ambition. A young man without a settled home decides to explain the whole Mishnah to ordinary readers, in their own language. And on the last page he asks forgiveness for his mistakes. Ambition and humility, bound into one book. Young and ambitious.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ARABIC, IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · `THE BEGINNER'S QUESTIONS, ANSWERED.` · `INTRODUCTIONS THAT ARE DOORWAYS.` · `AMBITION AND HUMILITY TOGETHER.` · then, large: `YOUNG AND AMBITIOUS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to begin one long project. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something you've meant to do for a long time: a book to read, a skill to learn, a text to study, a letter that will need many drafts. Don't plan all of it. Picture only the first step, small enough to do this week. Maimonides didn't wait for a quiet room or a settled life. Hold that first step for a few breaths. Then let it rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Commentary on the Mishnah. Perush HaMishnayot. Maimonides' early book explaining the Mishnah passage by passage, written in Arabic while he was on the move. Today's word.
Your line: young and ambitious. Today, take the first small step on your long project, even five minutes of it, and write down where you stopped. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Students of the Mishnah often read Maimonides' commentary, in Hebrew translation, alongside the text; his introductions, such as the one to Pirkei Avot, are also studied on their own.

fork.reveal: Maimonides begins on the move, writes in Arabic so people can use it, and apologizes at the end for any mistakes.
